idiom_name: hand-written vtable with a clone slot (`struct ShapeVtbl { Shape *(*clone)(const Shape *); }`)
implementation_notes: C has no inheritance, no virtual dispatch and no copy constructors, so the classic structure must be built by hand: a struct of function pointers (the virtual table) plus a vptr member in every instance - the emulation used by Samek's OOP-in-C and by GObject class structs, where virtual functions are function-pointer fields installed in `class_init`. Each concrete type installs its own clone function in its constructor, and the function must state an ownership rule (caller frees, refcount, or arena). What replaces the classic structure in most C APIs is a plain per-type copy function called directly (`gdk_pixbuf_copy`, `cJSON_Duplicate`-style `Shape_clone(const Shape *)`); route it through the vtbl only when the caller genuinely holds only the base 'interface'.
pitfalls: Plain struct assignment (or `memcpy`) copies the vptr and every pointer field, so the 'copy' still shares owned memory with the original - deep copies must duplicate each owned pointer and reinstall the concrete vtable.

C has no virtual destructor: unless the vtable also carries a destroy/free slot, freeing the clone through the base type leaks or corrupts the derived state, and the vtbl pointer of a derived object may be overwritten by an invalid one.
The allocation contract must be explicit and uniform (caller frees, refcount, or arena): mixing `malloc`-in-clone with a refcounted API (GLib-style) is how C clone functions leak or double-free.
